focus: Section 6, Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy. Explain discrete entropy using a small probability distribution. Let the learner change the distribution and the number of outcomes. Show probabilities, individual contributions, and total entropy in bits. Compare a certain outcome with equally likely outcomes. Check that certainty gives zero bits and four equally likely outcomes give two bits; handle zero probabilities correctly.
excerpt: Section 6 (paraphrased). Suppose one of n possible events will occur, with probabilities p1, p2, ..., pn, and these probabilities are all we know. We want a measure H(p1, ..., pn) of how much choice is involved, i.e. how uncertain we are of the outcome. Reasonable requirements are: H should be continuous in the pi; if all pi are equal (pi = 1/n), H should increase monotonically with n, since more equally likely events mean more choice; and if a choice is broken down into two successive choices, the original H should be the weighted sum of the individual values of H. Theorem 2: the only H satisfying these three assumptions has the form H = -K sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i log p_i, where K is a positive constant that merely fixes the unit of measure. Such quantities are called entropy. Choosing logarithms to base 2 measures H in bits. Properties: H = 0 if and only if all pi but one are zero and that one equals one, i.e. only when we are certain of the outcome; otherwise H is positive. For given n, H is largest and equal to log n when all pi are equal to 1/n, the most uncertain situation. For two possibilities with probabilities p and q = 1 - p, H = -(p log p + q log q). Terms with p = 0 contribute nothing (p log p tends to 0 as p tends to 0).
